rows.question: When does my maternity leave start if my due date is 15 November 2026?
rows.reply:
Under German law, the Mutterschutz (statutory maternity protection period) before birth covers the last six weeks before the birth. The law says your employer may not employ you "in den letzten sechs Wochen vor der Entbindung" unless you expressly declare that you are willing to work. You can withdraw that declaration at any time for the future.

The six weeks are counted back from the expected date of birth as stated in a certificate from your doctor or midwife ("der voraussichtliche Tag der Entbindung ... wie er sich aus dem ärztlichen Zeugnis oder dem Zeugnis einer Hebamme ... ergibt"). If that certificate gives 15 November 2026, the period starts six weeks before that date, in early October 2026. The excerpts do not set out how the first day is counted, so they do not fix the exact calendar day.

If the baby is not born on the expected date, the period before the birth becomes shorter or longer to match. After the birth, your employer may not employ you for eight weeks. This becomes twelve weeks for premature births and multiple births. If the baby comes early, the period after the birth is extended by the time lost before it.

The law says a pregnant woman should tell her employer about the pregnancy and the expected date of birth as soon as she knows. If the employer asks, she should provide a certificate from a doctor or midwife showing that date.

These rules apply to people in employment. The excerpts do not say who confirms the exact start date in a particular case. The certificate with your expected date of birth is what the calculation rests on, and your employer is the one bound by the employment ban.

rows.question: How long after birth can we apply for Elterngeld without losing money?
rows.reply:
The law does not set a deadline for applying for Elterngeld (parental allowance). It limits how far back payment goes.

Elterngeld can be received from the day of birth (BEEG §4(1): "Es kann ab dem Tag der Geburt bezogen werden"). It is paid in monthly amounts for the months of the child's life (BEEG §4(2)).

Payment is backdated only for the three months of the child's life before the month of the child's life in which your application arrives. The source says it is paid "rückwirkend nur für die letzten drei Lebensmonate vor Beginn des Lebensmonats ..., in dem der Antrag auf Elterngeld eingegangen ist" (BEEG §7(1)). Earlier months of the child's life are not paid. What counts is when the application is received, not when it is sent. The application must be made in writing ("schriftlich zu beantragen", BEEG §7(1)).

The same three-month limit applies if you later change the months you chose in the application (BEEG §7(2)).

Your Elterngeldstelle handles Elterngeld and decides your individual case. The excerpts do not say which Elterngeldstelle covers your address in Hessen. Ask your local authority, or check the Hessen state portal, to find the one responsible for you.

rows.question: How much notice do I have to give my employer for Elternzeit?
rows.reply:
The notice period depends on when the Elternzeit (parental leave (unpaid job-protected leave)) falls:

- For leave before your child's third birthday, you must request it from your employer at the latest seven weeks before it starts ("spätestens sieben Wochen … vor Beginn der Elternzeit").
- For leave between the third birthday and the end of the child's eighth year, the period is at least 13 weeks before it starts ("spätestens 13 Wochen").

The request must be made in text form ("in Textform"). According to the Familienportal, a letter without a signature or an email is enough. There is no application form. Elternzeit is requested from your employer, not from an authority.

When you request Elternzeit for the period before the third birthday, you must also state which periods within two years you will take. If the mother takes Elternzeit straight after her maternity protection period, that period counts toward these two years.

In urgent cases, an appropriately shorter notice period is possible as an exception ("Bei dringenden Gründen ist ausnahmsweise eine angemessene kürzere Frist möglich"). The Familienportal gives premature births as an example. It says the period that applies then depends on the individual case.

Your employer must confirm your Elternzeit to you.

The Familienportal also mentions a different notice rule for children born before a certain date. The statutory provision for those older cases is not in the material here. If that could apply to you, check the full text of the BEEG or ask your employer's HR department.

rows.question: How long is maternity protection after the birth if the baby comes early?
rows.reply:
The answer depends on whether the baby counts as a premature birth or was simply born before the expected date.

Normally, Mutterschutz (statutory maternity protection period) after the birth lasts eight weeks. During this time the employer may not employ the mother.

If the baby is born before the expected date but is not a premature birth, the period after the birth is extended. It gains the days that were lost from the six-week period before the birth. The law says: "Bei vorzeitiger Entbindung verlängert sich die Schutzfrist nach der Entbindung ... um den Zeitraum der Verkürzung der Schutzfrist vor der Entbindung." The Familienportal explains that the total Mutterschutz therefore still comes to 14 weeks.

If the birth is a premature birth ("bei Frühgeburten" in the law), the period after the birth is extended to twelve weeks. It is then extended further by the days lost from the period before the birth. The Familienportal gives an example of a birth that counts medically as premature: a baby weighing less than 2,500 grams at birth. It says the total Mutterschutz then rises from 14 weeks to 18 weeks. The statute itself does not define a premature birth.

After the birth, the mother may not work even if she wants to. The exception is for school pupils and students, who may resume their studies if they expressly ask to.

The excerpts do not say who decides whether a particular birth counts as premature. They do say that if an employer requires work during the Mutterschutz, the mother can contact the supervisory authority (Aufsichtsbehörde).

rows.question: Can my employer dismiss me while I am pregnant?
rows.reply:
In general, no. During pregnancy, dismissal by the employer is not allowed ("Die Kündigung gegenüber einer Frau ist unzulässig ... während ihrer Schwangerschaft"). This Kündigungsschutz (protection against dismissal) also runs until the end of the protection period after the birth, and at least until four months after the birth. It also covers four months after a miscarriage after the twelfth week of pregnancy.

The protection applies if the employer knows about the pregnancy at the time of dismissal, or is told within two weeks after receiving the dismissal ("innerhalb von zwei Wochen nach Zugang der Kündigung"). Missing the two weeks does no harm if it was not the woman's fault and she informs the employer without delay. The official guidance adds that she must already have been pregnant when the dismissal was received, even if she did not yet know.

There are narrow exceptions. The state's highest authority for occupational safety, or a body it designates, may declare a dismissal permissible in special cases that are not connected with the pregnancy, a miscarriage or the birth. Such a dismissal must be in writing and must state the reason. The official guidance gives examples such as insolvency, partial closure of the business, or a particularly serious breach of duty. It also states that without the supervisory authority's consent, the dismissal is invalid ("unwirksam").

If you are dismissed without that consent, the official guidance says you must bring a claim before the labour court. It says the claim must "normalerweise innerhalb von 3 Wochen" (normally within 3 weeks) be filed, counted from receipt of the written dismissal. If no claim is filed, the dismissal counts as valid. You can file the claim yourself, through a lawyer, or orally at the court office. The guidance also says you should involve the supervisory authority.

If you take parental leave after the birth, the protection can be extended.

Whether a particular dismissal is valid is not something this service can assess. The labour court decides that. The supervisory authority for maternity protection in your state decides whether a dismissal is permitted as an exception.

rows.question: Is there an income limit above which we get no Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes. The law sets an income limit above which there is no entitlement to Elterngeld (parental allowance). The limit is based on zu versteuerndes Einkommen (taxable income), not gross pay.

What the statute says (BEEG §1 Absatz 8):
- For one entitled person, the entitlement lapses if their zu versteuerndes Einkommen in the last completed tax assessment period before the birth was more than 175,000 euros ("in Höhe von mehr als 175 000 Euro").
- If another person also meets the conditions, typically the other parent, the entitlement lapses if the two incomes added together are more than 175,000 euros ("wenn die Summe des zu versteuernden Einkommens beider Personen mehr als 175 000 Euro beträgt").

The federal family portal explains that zu versteuerndes Einkommen is usually well below gross income. Special expenses, pension and insurance contributions, individual allowances and extraordinary burdens are deducted first. The figure is set by the Finanzamt and appears in the tax assessment notice.

If the tax assessment notice is not yet available when the application is made, the statute provides for a provisional decision. Payment is made subject to revocation if the limit later turns out to be exceeded (BEEG §8 Absatz 2 and 3).

Earlier births: the official guidance says different, higher limits applied to children born before 1 April 2025. The statute's transitional provision for earlier births is not among the sources I have, so I cannot say which rule applies to a particular birth.

Whether the limit applies to your family is decided by the Elterngeld office responsible for where you live, not by this guide. In Hessen, the application is made to that state Elterngeld office, which can also tell you which income rule applies to your child's birth.

rows.question: How many months of Elterngeld can we get in total?
rows.reply:
The law sets the number of monthly payments for both parents together. How many apply to your family is decided by your Elterngeld office, not here.

The basic rule: parents together are entitled to twelve monthly payments of basic Elterngeld (parental allowance): "Die Eltern haben gemeinsam Anspruch auf zwölf Monatsbeträge Basiselterngeld."

Two extra months: if one parent's income from work is reduced in two months of the child's life, the parents together get two more months: "zwei weitere Monate Basiselterngeld (Partnermonate)". That makes 14 in total.

The Plus variant: instead of one month of the basic variant, a parent can take two months of Elterngeld Plus: "Statt für einen Lebensmonat Basiselterngeld zu beanspruchen, kann die berechtigte Person jeweils zwei Lebensmonate Elterngeld Plus beziehen." This spreads payments over more months.

Partnership bonus: on top of this, each parent can get up to four more monthly payments: "zuzüglich der höchstens vier zustehenden Monatsbeträge Partnerschaftsbonus nach § 4b". The Familienportal explains this is for parents who both work part-time at the same time.

Limits for each parent:
- One parent can get at most twelve monthly payments of the basic variant: "höchstens zwölf Monatsbeträge Basiselterngeld".
- A parent only gets Elterngeld if they take it for at least two months: "mindestens für zwei Lebensmonate".
- Payments are made for months of the child's life, counted from the birth date, not calendar months.

Time windows:
- The basic variant can be taken until the child completes the 14th month of life.
- Elterngeld Plus can be taken until the child completes the 32nd month of life, as long as from the 15th month at least one parent takes it in consecutive months. The Familienportal adds that if there is a month after the 14th in which neither parent receives it, none can be received afterwards, even if months are left.

Premature births: for a child born at least six weeks before the expected date, the joint entitlement rises to 13 monthly payments of the basic variant. It is 14 at eight weeks early, 15 at twelve weeks, and 16 at 16 weeks. The expected date shown in the doctor's or midwife's certificate is what counts.

Months in which certain other benefits are paid count as months of the basic variant. The Familienportal names maternity benefits (Mutterschaftsgeld) as an example. So these months are used up whether or not you apply for them.

Which of these rules apply to your family, and how many months you receive, is decided by the Elterngeld office responsible for where you live. You submit your application there, and that is where you can get binding information about your own case.

rows.question: What is the Partnerschaftsbonus and who qualifies?
rows.reply:
The Partnerschaftsbonus (partnership bonus months) is an extra payment under federal parental allowance law for parents who both work part-time at the same time.

What the law says:

- Each parent gets an additional monthly amount of the Plus variant of parental allowance for each month of the child's life in which both parents work on average "nicht weniger als 24 und nicht mehr als 32 Wochenstunden im Durchschnitt des Lebensmonats" (no fewer than 24 and no more than 32 hours a week, averaged over that month of the child's life). Both parents must also meet the general conditions of BEEG §1. Those conditions are not set out in the excerpts available here. (BEEG §4b(1))
- Each parent can receive at most four monthly amounts. The bonus can only be drawn if it is taken for at least two months of the child's life. (BEEG §4b(2))
- The parents can only draw it at the same time and in consecutive months of the child's life. (BEEG §4b(3))
- If, during the bonus, one of the single-parent situations in BEEG §4c(1) nos. 1 to 3 arises, one parent can continue the bonus alone. (BEEG §4b(4))
- The consecutive-months requirement still counts as met if it later turns out that the conditions were not met in every month for which the bonus was applied for. (BEEG §4b(5))

One parent alone:
A parent can claim these additional amounts alone where one of the situations in BEEG §4c(1) applies. Those situations are:

- the parent meets the conditions for the tax relief for single parents, and the other parent lives neither with them nor with the child;
- care by the other parent would endanger the child's welfare;
- care by the other parent is impossible, for example because of serious illness or severe disability.

That parent must work on average 24 to 32 hours a week in at least two and at most four consecutive months of the child's life. (BEEG §4c(1) and (2))

What the official guidance adds:
The federal family portal says the following:

- The bonus is calculated the same way as the Plus variant. Depending on income before the birth, it is between 150 and 900 euros a month per parent.
- If either parent works fewer than 24 or more than 32 hours in a month, the bonus for that month must be repaid, and both parents lose it for that month.
- Payments for the other months are kept as long as the conditions are met in at least two months.

The portal also says its explanations cover children born after August 2021. For children born before 1 September 2021, partly different rules apply, and it refers those parents to the parental allowance office.

Whether your family qualifies, and for how many months, is decided by the parental allowance office (Elterngeldstelle) responsible for where you live. That is also where the application is submitted. The excerpts do not name the specific office in Hessen.

rows.question: We forgot to apply for Kindergeld. How far back will they pay?
rows.reply:
The law limits back payment of Kindergeld (child benefit) to six months. Kindergeld is paid retroactively only for the last six months before the start of the month in which the application is received ("rückwirkend nur für die letzten sechs Monate vor Beginn des Monats, in dem der Antrag auf Kindergeld eingegangen ist"). Months further back than that are not paid out. The same provision says the underlying entitlement itself is not affected by this payment limit.

The law does not set an application deadline here. The consequence of applying late is that months more than six months before the month your application arrives are not paid.

Kindergeld must be applied for in writing, and the application should be made to the responsible family benefits office. The official family portal says to make the application at the family benefits office of your Agentur für Arbeit. When applying retroactively, it says to state in the application that you are applying retroactively and from when you want to receive Kindergeld.

Whether your family is entitled, and for which months, is decided by the family benefits office, not by this service. The Federal Employment Agency's free service line for questions about applying is 0800 4 555530.

rows.question: How quickly do we have to register the birth at the Standesamt?
rows.reply:
The birth must be reported within one week. The Personenstandsgesetz (civil status law) says the birth of a child must be reported to the Standesamt (civil registry office) for the place where the child was born "binnen einer Woche" (within one week).

If your child is born in a hospital, birth centre or maternity clinic, the facility notifies the responsible Standesamt and sends it the birth certificate issued at the birth. If your child is born at home, the midwife or doctor issues that certificate, and you must present it to the responsible Standesamt within one week.

The official checklist on the same family portal says "innerhalb von 7 Werktagen" (within 7 working days). The law itself says one week. If the difference matters to you, ask the Standesamt for the place of birth.

The Standesamt for the place of birth handles the registration. Which other documents you need is listed on that Standesamt's website.

If you have not yet chosen a name, you must tell the responsible Standesamt within one month. After that, the Standesamt is required to inform the family court, which then decides which parent sets the name.

rows.question: Which Standesamt do we go to — the one where we live or where the hospital is?
rows.reply:
The Standesamt (civil registry office) responsible for the place where your child is born, so the one covering the hospital's location, not the one where you live.

The law says the birth must be reported to the Standesamt "in dessen Zuständigkeitsbereich es geboren ist" (in whose area the child was born), "binnen einer Woche" (within one week). The official family portal says the same: you register your child with the Standesamt "das für den Geburtsort des Kindes zuständig ist" (responsible for the child's place of birth).

If your child is born in a hospital, birth centre or maternity clinic, the facility notifies the responsible Standesamt and sends it the birth certificate issued at the birth. You give the child's first name and surname to the facility, which passes them on.

The portal says the list of other documents you need is on the website of the Standesamt in the town where your child is born.

rows.question: What do we need to bring to the Standesamt to register the birth?
rows.reply:
The one document the official source names is the certificate of birth issued by the hospital, midwife or doctor. The source says: "Für die Anmeldung beim Standesamt benötigen Sie die Geburtsbescheinigung" (to register at the Standesamt (civil registry office) you need the certificate of birth).

- Born in a hospital, birth centre or maternity clinic: the facility notifies the responsible Standesamt and sends the certificate of birth itself.
- Born at home: the midwife or doctor issues the certificate of birth, and you must present it to the responsible Standesamt within one week.

The law requires the birth to be reported within one week ("binnen einer Woche") to the Standesamt for the place where the child was born. Parents who report the birth themselves must credibly show that the birth took place ("die Geburt des Kindes glaubhaft zu machen").

If you are not married, the father is only entered on the birth certificate if he makes an acknowledgement of paternity at the Standesamt or the youth welfare office. This can also be done before the birth.

You can give someone written authority to handle these visits to offices for you.

rows.question: Does my Krankenkasse pay for a midwife?
rows.reply:
Under federal statutory health insurance law, a woman insured with a Krankenkasse (statutory health insurer) is entitled to midwife care during pregnancy, at the birth and after the birth. This includes the examinations to confirm the pregnancy and prenatal check-ups.

Midwife care for the period after the birth (the Wochenbett) runs until twelve weeks after the birth ("bis zum Ablauf von zwölf Wochen nach der Geburt"). Further care beyond that needs a doctor's order ("bedürfen der ärztlichen Anordnung").

If the mother cannot care for the baby after the birth, the insured child is entitled to the midwife care that relates to the child.

The official family portal puts it the same way: every woman with statutory health insurance has a right to support from a Hebamme (midwife). If you are privately insured, the portal says to check with your insurer beforehand which services it covers.

What is covered in your own case is decided by your Krankenkasse, or by your private insurer if you are privately insured. Contact them directly for binding information.

rows.question: How do we insure the baby after the birth?
rows.reply:
Under federal law, a child can be covered through Familienversicherung (free family cover for dependants) in statutory health insurance. The law says the children of members are insured ("Versichert sind ... die Kinder von Mitgliedern") if the child meets these conditions:

- lives or usually stays in Germany ("Wohnsitz oder gewöhnlichen Aufenthalt im Inland")
- is not insured in their own right and is not voluntarily insured
- is not exempt from compulsory insurance
- is not self-employed as a main occupation
- has no total income regularly above one seventh of the monthly reference amount ("ein Siebtel der monatlichen Bezugsgröße").

Children are covered up to their 18th birthday ("bis zur Vollendung des achtzehnten Lebensjahres"). Cover can continue longer in some cases, for example during school or vocational training.

There is one exception that matters for many families. The child is not covered through Familienversicherung if the other parent is not a member of a statutory health insurance fund ("nicht Mitglied einer Krankenkasse"), and that parent's total income regularly exceeds one twelfth of the annual earnings ceiling ("ein Zwölftel der Jahresarbeitsentgeltgrenze"), and is regularly higher than the member parent's income. The excerpts do not say how the child is insured in that case.

The practical step the excerpts describe starts with the birth certificate. You must register the birth with the registry office for the place of birth within 1 week. The registry office issues the birth certificate. The birth certificate is needed to register the child with the health insurance fund. If the baby is born in a hospital, birth centre or maternity clinic, the facility notifies the registry office.

The excerpts do not cover the forms or timing for registering with the health insurance fund. They also do not cover private health insurance. Ask your statutory health insurance fund how to register the baby. Only the fund decides whether your child is covered through Familienversicherung.

rows.question: When are the first check-ups for the baby?
rows.reply: The Kinder-Richtlinie sets ten check-ups in the first six years of life. The first ones are: U1, right after birth ("Unmittelbar nach der Geburt"). It should be done within the first 30 minutes after the baby is born. If no doctor is present at the birth but a midwife is, the midwife should do it. U2, between the 3rd and 10th day of life, with a tolerance limit of the 3rd to 14th day ("3.-10. Lebenstag", tolerance "3.-14. Lebenstag"). U3, in the 4th to 5th week of life, with a tolerance limit of the 3rd to 8th week ("4.-5. Lebenswoche", tolerance "3.-8. Lebenswoche"). U4, in the 3rd to 4th month of life, with a tolerance limit of the 2nd to 4.5th month. U5, in the 6th to 7th month, with a tolerance limit of the 5th to 8th month. U6, in the 10th to 12th month, with a tolerance limit of the 9th to 14th month. The guideline says the check-ups can only be used within these periods, taking the tolerance limits into account ("können nur in den jeweils angegebenen Zeiträumen unter Berücksichtigung folgender Toleranzgrenzen in Anspruch genommen werden"). The same periods apply to babies born early. Being born early is taken into account when the results are assessed.

rows.question: What is Mutterschaftsgeld and when do I apply for it?
rows.reply:
Mutterschaftsgeld (maternity pay from the health insurer) is a payment for the maternity protection periods before and after the birth, and for the day of birth itself. A woman who is a member of a statutory health insurer receives it under the rules of Social Code Book V (MuSchG §19(1)). The official family portal says these protection periods normally begin 6 weeks before the expected due date and end 8 weeks after the birth.

Who receives it from the health insurer: members who are entitled to sick pay if unable to work, or who receive no pay from their employer because of the protection periods (SGB V §24i(1)).

How the amount is set: for members employed when the protection period before the birth begins, it is the average daily net pay of the last three settled calendar months before that period, capped at 13 euros per calendar day ("höchstens 13 Euro für den Kalendertag"). If average daily pay is higher, the employer pays the difference as a supplement (SGB V §24i(2), MuSchG §20(1)).

If you are not a member of a statutory health insurer, Mutterschaftsgeld is paid by the federal government, at most 210 euros in total ("insgesamt höchstens 210 Euro"). It is paid on application ("auf Antrag") by the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung (MuSchG §19(2)).

When to apply: the excerpts do not say when to apply. They say only that for payment before the birth, the decisive document is a certificate from a doctor or midwife stating the expected day of delivery (SGB V §24i(3)). For when and how to apply, ask your statutory health insurer. If you are not statutorily insured, ask the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung.

Good to know: Mutterschaftsgeld under Social Code Book V, and the employer supplement, are offset against parental allowance for the period from the day of birth. The 210-euro payment from the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung is not offset (BEEG §3(1)).

Whether you qualify, and how much you would receive, is decided by your health insurer or, if you are not statutorily insured, by the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung.

rows.question: We are not married. Is my partner automatically the legal father?
rows.reply:
No. Under German law, a man is the legal father of a child in one of three ways: he is married to the mother at the time of the birth, he has acknowledged paternity, or a court has determined his paternity (BGB §1592).

If you are not married to each other when the child is born, your partner becomes the legal father through a Vaterschaftsanerkennung (acknowledgement of paternity). The acknowledgement is voluntary, and the mother must consent to it.

What the law and official guidance say about it:

- It can be made before the child is born (BGB §1594(4): "Die Anerkennung ist schon vor der Geburt des Kindes zulässig").
- It cannot be made subject to a condition or a time limit. Such an acknowledgement is invalid (BGB §1594(3)).
- It does not take effect while another man is the legal father (BGB §1594(2)). For example, if the mother is married to another man at the birth, her husband is the legal father.
- Its legal effects apply only from the moment it becomes effective (BGB §1594(1)).
- Your partner must make the declaration in person at a competent office, for example the youth welfare office, a registry office, a local court or a notary. The mother must also give her consent in person. The office records both. Depending on the federal state, a notary or local court may charge a fee.

If the father does not want to acknowledge paternity, or the mother does not consent, the child, the mother or the presumed biological father can ask a court to determine paternity.

Acknowledging paternity does not on its own give your partner parental custody. If you are not married at the birth, the mother has custody. For joint custody, both parents must also declare that they want to share custody, or a court must decide. Marrying after the birth also establishes joint custody.

The youth welfare office advises on paternity and custody questions.

rows.question: How do unmarried parents get joint custody?
rows.reply:
If the parents are not married to each other when the child is born, the mother has parental custody alone at first. Under federal law, the parents get joint custody in one of three ways (BGB §1626a(1)):

1. Both parents declare that they want to take on custody jointly. These declarations are called Sorgeerklärungen. A Sorgeerklärung (declaration of joint custody) can be made, for example, at the youth welfare office or before a notary, and can be made before the birth ("Sorgeerklärungen können auch schon vor der Geburt abgegeben werden").

2. The parents marry each other, including after the birth.

3. The family court transfers custody to both parents jointly. One parent can apply for this. The court does so if joint custody does not contradict the child's welfare ("dem Kindeswohl nicht widerspricht"). If the other parent puts forward no reasons against it, and none are otherwise apparent, the law presumes that joint custody does not contradict the child's welfare (BGB §1626a(2)). The official family portal adds that in this case the court decides in a simplified procedure, without hearing the youth welfare office and without a personal hearing of the parents.

For the father, legal paternity comes first. He becomes the legal father by acknowledging the child as his own with the mother's consent, or through a court finding of paternity. Acknowledging paternity does not by itself give him custody. A Sorgeerklärung or a court decision is still needed.

If none of these routes applies, the mother keeps custody alone (BGB §1626a(3)).

Your local youth welfare office advises on all questions of parental custody. Whether joint custody is transferred in a particular case is decided by the family court.

rows.question: Where do we apply for Elterngeld in Frankfurt?
rows.reply:
You apply to the Elterngeldstelle (the state office that decides parental allowance) responsible for where your child lives. The law says the responsible office is the one for the district where the child has its residence in Germany when you first apply ("des Bezirks, in dem das Kind ... zum Zeitpunkt der ersten Antragstellung seinen inländischen Wohnsitz hat"). Which office that is gets decided by each state: "Die Landesregierungen ... bestimmen die für die Ausführung dieses Gesetzes zuständigen Behörden." For a child living in Frankfurt, that means the office Hessen has designated for Frankfurt.

The excerpts I have do not name the Hessen office or its address. The official Familienportal says you can find the responsible Elterngeldstelle under its "Beratung vor Ort" (local advice) search.

How you can apply:
- In person at the Elterngeldstelle, or digitally. The Familienportal says every state offers a digital application ("Es gibt in allen Bundesländern die Möglichkeit, Elterngeld digital zu beantragen").
- The application must be in writing ("Elterngeld ist schriftlich zu beantragen").
- Payment is backdated for at most the three months of the child's life before the month the office receives your application. Earlier months are not paid, so applying late costs whole months of Elterngeld.

Whether you qualify, and for how much, is decided by your Elterngeldstelle.

rows.question: Where do we apply for Elterngeld in Berlin?
rows.reply:
You apply to the Elterngeldstelle (the state office that decides parental allowance) responsible for where your child lives. Under federal law, each state decides which authority handles Elterngeld (parental allowance). The responsible office is the one for the district where the child has its residence in Germany when you first apply ("des Bezirks, in dem das Kind ... zum Zeitpunkt der ersten Antragstellung seinen inländischen Wohnsitz hat").

The application must be made in writing ("Elterngeld ist schriftlich zu beantragen"). In it, you state which months you are claiming Basiselterngeld, Elterngeld Plus or Partnerschaftsbonus for. Except for single parents with sole custody and the case in § 4c, the parent applying signs it. The other parent also signs to confirm they have seen it.

In Berlin you can apply in two ways:
- Through Service Berlin online. To do this, you log in with a BundID account or register for one. Logging in with the online ID function of an electronic ID card or residence permit (eAT) is recommended. An Elster certificate or a username and password are alternatives.
- Through ElterngeldDigital, which covers Berlin. A digital assistant helps you fill in the form. You then print it, sign it and post it to your responsible Elterngeldstelle. The ElterngeldDigital support hotline is 0421 - 361 94195, Monday to Thursday, 10-12 and 13-15.

The Service Berlin page lists being resident and registered in Berlin ("Sie wohnen in Berlin und sind hier gemeldet") as a condition. Your Elterngeldstelle decides whether you meet the conditions.

Timing matters. Payment is made retroactively only for the three months of the child's life before the month in which the application is received. Earlier months are not paid.

rows.question: Will our baby automatically be German if we are both Indian citizens?
rows.reply:
Whether your baby becomes German is decided for the individual case, not by us. Here is what the law says.

German Staatsangehörigkeit (citizenship) is acquired by birth if one parent holds German Staatsangehörigkeit.

For a child of foreign parents born in Germany, there is a separate rule. The child acquires German Staatsangehörigkeit by birth in Germany if one parent meets both of these conditions:
1. has lawfully had their habitual residence in Germany for five years ("seit fünf Jahren rechtmäßig seinen gewöhnlichen Aufenthalt im Inland"), and
2. holds an unlimited right of residence ("ein unbefristetes Aufenthaltsrecht"), or, for Swiss citizens and their family members, a residence permit under the EU–Switzerland free movement agreement.

So being born in Germany is not enough on its own. The law attaches these conditions to at least one parent. Where the child acquires citizenship this way, it is entered in the birth register in which the child's birth is recorded.

There is also a rule on residence for children born in Germany who are not German. If both parents, or the parent with sole custody, hold a residence permit, a settlement permit or an EU long-term residence permit at the time of the birth, the child is granted a residence permit automatically. If only one parent holds one of these, the child may be granted one. If a parent holds a visa or may stay without a visa, the child's stay counts as permitted until that visa or visa-free stay ends.

Who decides: the excerpts do not name the office that confirms citizenship in your case. Ask the registry office that registers your baby's birth and keeps the birth register. That office records acquisition of citizenship. The excerpts say nothing about Indian citizenship for your baby. For that, contact the Indian embassy or consulate responsible for where you live.

rows.question: We are getting Mutterschaftsgeld. Does that reduce our Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes, as a general rule. Mutterschaftsgeld (maternity pay from the health insurer) from a statutory health insurer, and the employer's top-up to it under MuSchG §20, are offset against Elterngeld (parental allowance) for the time from the day of the child's birth. The statute lists these among the income that "auf das ... Elterngeld ... angerechnet" is (BEEG §3(1) no. 1).

There is one exception. The one-off Mutterschaftsgeld of at most 210 euros paid by the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung to women who are not members of a statutory health insurer (MuSchG §19(2)) is not offset (BEEG §3(1) no. 1 a).

What the offset means, according to the federal family portal:
- Maternity benefits for the same child are offset in full ("komplett auf das Elterngeld angerechnet"). If they are higher than the Elterngeld, only the maternity benefits are paid. If the Elterngeld is higher, the difference is paid as Elterngeld.
- Months in which the mother is entitled to these benefits for the same child count as months of Basiselterngeld for her, even if the entitlement covers only one day of that month.
- The offset is calculated by the day. If the benefits stop partway through a month of the child's life, Elterngeld is paid for the remaining days of that month. The statute says the same: income received for only part of a month is offset only against the matching part of the Elterngeld (BEEG §3(1), sentence after no. 5).
- The mother's maternity benefits are not offset against the father's Elterngeld. They are offset only against the mother's.
- If the maternity benefits are for a different, younger child, they are offset against only part of the Elterngeld. 300 euros per month of Basiselterngeld, or 150 euros per month of ElterngeldPlus, is not offset.

How much Elterngeld you will actually receive after the offset is decided by the Elterngeld office responsible for where you live. Your application for Elterngeld goes to that office. These excerpts do not name the office for your district.

rows.question: Can I work while receiving Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes, working is possible within limits. One condition of the entitlement to Elterngeld (parental allowance) is that the person does no work or does not work full time: "keine oder keine volle Erwerbstätigkeit ausübt" (BEEG §1(1) no. 4).

The federal explanatory page puts the limit at no more than 32 hours a week: "nicht mehr als 32 Stunden pro Woche". The same page says its explanations apply to children born after August 2021, and that partly different rules apply to children born earlier. Which rules apply to a particular birth is decided by your local Elterngeld office.

Working affects the amount. The full rate, up to 1,800 euros a month, applies to months in which the person has no income from work (BEEG §2(1)). For months after the birth with income from work that is lower than income before the birth, Elterngeld is paid as a percentage of the difference between the two. For this calculation, pre-birth income counts up to at most 2,770 euros (BEEG §2(3)).

What you state in the application matters:
- If you state expected income from work, the decision on the amount is provisional (BEEG §8(3) no. 3). After the benefit period ends, you must prove your actual income from work for that time (BEEG §8(1)).
- If you state you will have no income from work, Elterngeld is paid subject to revocation if you do have such income (BEEG §8(2)).

The explanatory page also lists proof of working hours during the benefit period. Employees need a certificate from their employer. Self-employed people need their own statement of past working hours and of working hours during the benefit period.

How much you would receive while working is not something this answer can assess. Your local Elterngeld office decides your individual case.

rows.question: Where and how do we apply for Kindergeld?
rows.reply:
Where to apply: The law says the application should go to the responsible family benefits office ("Familienkasse"). That is the office for the district where the entitled person lives ("in deren Bezirk der Berechtigte seinen Wohnsitz hat"). The official family portal says this is usually the Familienkasse of your local employment agency ("Familienkasse Ihrer Agentur für Arbeit").

How to apply: Kindergeld (child benefit) must be applied for in writing ("schriftlich zu beantragen"). The family portal says you can apply electronically or in writing, using the Familienkasse form. You can fill the form in online, then print and sign it. For a newborn, you can apply fully online with a valid ELSTER certificate, without printing or signing by hand.

What to include: The application must state your tax identification number and your child's tax identification number. For a child under 18, these numbers are usually all you need to provide. If your child was born abroad or lives abroad, submit a copy of the foreign birth certificate, or another official document certifying the birth. If the office needs more documents, it will tell you and set a date. If you miss that date, your application may be delayed or refused.

Who applies: Kindergeld goes to only one person per child. If the child lives in the parents' shared household, the parents decide between themselves who is the entitled person. Besides the entitled person, anyone with a legitimate interest in the payment may also apply.

Applying late: The family portal says Kindergeld can be paid retroactively for up to 6 months. If you apply retroactively, state this in the application and say from when you want to receive it.

Questions: The Federal Employment Agency has a free service line for application questions: 0800 4 555530. The Familienkasse decides on each claim.

rows.question: What are the Elterngeld rules for a self-employed parent in Bavaria?
rows.reply:
Bavarian state procedures are outside what this service covers. Your search covered federal law, Hessen procedures and the Indian consular track, not Bavaria. The federal Elterngeld (parental allowance) rules below come from the Federal Parental Allowance and Parental Leave Act (BEEG). They apply everywhere in Germany, including Bavaria.

Who can claim. You must live or usually stay in Germany, live in one household with the child, care for and raise the child yourself, and work not at all or not full-time (BEEG §1(1)).

How self-employed income counts. Elterngeld is 67 percent of income from work before the birth. That income includes positive earnings from "Land- und Forstwirtschaft, Gewerbebetrieb und selbständiger Arbeit" (farming and forestry, trade or business, and self-employed work) that are taxable in Germany. Taxes and social contributions are deducted, and the income is averaged per month over the statute's assessment period (BEEG §2(1)). The percentage rises if pre-birth income was under 1,000 euros and falls to as low as 65 percent if it was over 1,200 euros (BEEG §2(2)). The maximum is 1,800 euros a month for full months with no income from work (BEEG §2(1)). The minimum is 300 euros (BEEG §2(4)). If you earn less than before during the months you receive Elterngeld, it is paid on the difference, with pre-birth income counted up to 2,770 euros at most (BEEG §2(3)).

Provisional decisions and proof. The amount is decided provisionally in three cases (BEEG §8(3)):
- the tax assessment notice for the last completed tax period before the birth is not available when you apply;
- your pre-birth income cannot be determined;
- you expect to have income from work while receiving Elterngeld.

If you gave expected income in the application, you must prove your actual income for that period after the benefit period ends (BEEG §8(1)). If you stated you would have no income, Elterngeld is paid subject to revocation if you do have income (BEEG §8(2)).

How long. Basic Elterngeld can be received until the child completes the 14th month of life. Elterngeld Plus can run until the 32nd month under the conditions the statute sets. Two months of Elterngeld Plus can replace one month of the basic form (BEEG §4(1), §4(3)).

These excerpts do not say which documents to submit or how to apply in Bavaria. They also do not decide whether you qualify or how much you would get. Only the responsible Elterngeld office (Elterngeldstelle) in Bavaria decides your case. Apply there, and ask that office for binding information about your situation.

rows.question: Can you fill in our Elterngeld application form for us?
rows.reply:
We can't fill in your Elterngeld (parental allowance) application for you. Filling it in means deciding which months to claim, which option to choose and what to declare for your family, and that is an assessment of your individual case. Only the responsible authority decides your case. Here is what the rules say the application involves.

What the law requires of the application:
- Elterngeld must be applied for in writing.
- The application must state for which months of the child's life you are claiming basic Elterngeld, for which months the Plus variant, and for which months the partnership bonus.
- Payment is made retroactively only for the last three months of the child's life before the month in which the application is received. Earlier months are not paid.
- The person applying signs it. The other entitled parent also signs to confirm they have seen it, unless the applicant has sole custody or another listed exception applies. The other parent can submit their own application at the same time.
- The choices you make can be changed until the end of the payment period, with limits on changes to past months.

Documents the official family portal lists:
- your child's birth certificate
- proof of your previous income, for example pay slips for the 12 months before the relevant month, or your last tax assessment if you are self-employed
- certificates about maternity pay or employer top-ups, where they apply
- where relevant, proof of working hours or income while you receive Elterngeld
Further documents may be needed depending on the individual case. Your employer must issue the documents you need.

Who decides and where to go: the authority responsible is the one your Land designates for the district where your child lives at the time of the first application. That is your local Elterngeld office. Submit the application there, and ask it directly about how to complete the form for your situation. It can also advise on parental leave.

- lives in one household with the child

rows.question: How much tax will we save if I switch to Steuerklasse 3 before the birth?
rows.reply:
We cannot tell you how much tax you would save by switching tax class, or whether switching is a good idea for you. Choosing a tax class and working out its tax effect is individual tax advice. Only the tax office or a tax adviser can give it.

What the excerpts do cover is how a tax class change before the birth is treated when parental allowance is calculated:

- Parental allowance uses a simplified net income figure. When working out the tax deducted for that figure, the tax class is taken into account. Tax class VI is ignored ("die Steuerklasse VI bleibt unberücksichtigt").
- If you changed tax class before the birth, the newest tax class is used ("kommt es auf die neueste Steuerklasse an"). The older tax class is used only if it applied for longer than the newer one within the whole assessment period ("wenn diese innerhalb des gesamten Bemessungszeitraums länger gegolten hat als die neuere").
- Changing tax class again after the birth no longer has any effect on your parental allowance.

These rules do not tell you what your own parental allowance would be. The parental allowance office calculates the amount for your application and decides it.

Where to go next:

- For the tax saving and the choice of tax class, ask your tax office or a tax adviser.
- For how a change would affect your parental allowance, ask the parental allowance office responsible for where you live. You also submit your application there.
